lead: The uniform distribution gives equal probability density to every point in an interval. It models a random quantity with no preferred value inside fixed bounds: a train arrival, a rounding error, a random number between 0 and 1. On [a,b], the density is a flat rectangle of height 1/(b − a). Interval probability is interval length divided by b − a. The mean is the midpoint. Variance grows with the square of the interval width. Use it as a simple model and as the base for simulation.
prereq: You need: continuous random variables, pdf and CDF, and basic integration from Unit 2; the exponential distribution later replaces the flat density with a falling one.

blocks.text: A continuous random variable X is uniform on the interval [a,b] when every point in [a,b] has the same density. The word continuous matters: X can take any real value in the interval, not just whole numbers. The density is flat because no subinterval is favoured. Some syllabi call this the rectangular distribution, after the shape of its graph.
f(x) = 1/(b − a) for a ≤ x ≤ b; f(x) = 0 otherwise
blocks.where: a is the left end, b is the right end, a < b; b − a is the interval length; f(x) is the probability density at x, measured in probability per unit of x.

blocks.text: The total area under a density must be 1. The graph is a rectangle of width b − a and height h. Set h(b − a) = 1 to get h = 1/(b − a). For a wait W uniform on 0 to 10 minutes, the height is 1/10 = 0.1 per minute.

items: The density can be above 1 if b − a is less than 1. A density is not a probability.
The support is [a,b]. Outside it, the density is 0.

blocks.text: The cumulative distribution function F(x) gives P(X ≤ x). For a uniform variable it rises in a straight line from 0 at a to 1 at b.
F(x) = 0 for x < a; F(x) = (x − a)/(b − a) for a ≤ x ≤ b; F(x) = 1 for x > b
blocks.where: F(x) is the probability that X is at most x; a and b are the interval ends; x is the value at which you evaluate the CDF.

blocks.text: For any interval [c,d] inside [a,b], probability equals length divided by total length.

blocks.where: c is the lower endpoint, d is the upper endpoint, with a ≤ c ≤ d ≤ b; d − c is the interval length in the same units as X.

blocks.text: A single point has width 0. Its area is 0. So P(X = c) = 0 for every c. This makes P(X ≤ c) and P(X < c) equal. For W uniform on 0 to 10 minutes, P(W ≤ 3) = (3 − 0)/(10 − 0) = 0.3. Also P(W = 3) = 0. The events W ≤ 3 and W < 3 have the same probability.
By symmetry the average sits at the midpoint of the interval. The spread depends only on the interval length.

blocks.where: E(X) is the mean or expected value; a and b are the interval ends; the answer is in the same units as X.
Var(X) is the variance, in squared units of X; σ is the standard deviation, back in the original units; a and b are the interval ends.

blocks.text: For X uniform on 0 to 1, the mean is 0.5 and the variance is 1/12 ≈ 0.0833. For X uniform on 2 to 8, the mean is 5 and the variance is 36/12 = 3. The flat model fits a random arrival inside a fixed schedule, a rounding error with known bounds, and a random number from a generator. Simulation builds on uniform random numbers; a short note appears in the Beyond box at the end. When waits are more likely to be short than long, the exponential distribution is the better model.

figure.caption: The rectangle has height 0.1 per minute and width 10 minutes, so its area is 1. A strip from 0 to 3 minutes would have area 3 × 0.1 = 0.3.

spec.aria: A rectangle of height 0.1 from zero to ten minutes shows the uniform density of waiting times.

examples.question: A metro train runs every 10 minutes. You reach the platform at a random time, and your wait W in minutes is uniform on (0,10). (a) Find P(W ≤ 3). (b) Find E(W).
steps: Step 1: Set the model. W ~ U(0,10), so a = 0 min and b = 10 min. The density is f(w) = 1/10 = 0.1 per minute for 0 ≤ w ≤ 10, and 0 outside.
Step 2: Convert the event to an interval. P(W ≤ 3) = P(0 ≤ W ≤ 3). The endpoint 0 has probability 0, so include it freely.
Step 3: Use length over total length. Length = 3 − 0 = 3 min. Total length = 10 − 0 = 10 min. P = 3/10 = 0.3.
Step 4: Find the mean by the midpoint formula. E(W) = (0 + 10)/2 = 5 min.
examples.answer: P(W ≤ 3) = 0.3, and the expected wait is 5 minutes.
examples.check:
a = 0.0
b = 10.0
c = 0.0
d = 3.0
p = (d - c) / (b - a)
mean = (a + b) / 2
print(p)
print(mean)

traps: The height f(x) = 1/(b − a) is a density, not a probability. Probability comes from area, so P(X = c) = 0 for every single c.
For a continuous uniform variable, P(X ≤ c) = P(X < c) and P(X ≥ c) = P(X > c). Do not add a point mass at c.
Use the density 1/(b − a) only inside [a,b]. Outside, f(x) = 0. Writing 0.1 for a wait of 12 minutes on U(0,10) is wrong.
Variance is (b − a)²/12, with squared units. The standard deviation is (b − a)/√12, back in original units. Examiners often ask for both.
Discrete uniform on {1,...,n} gives each point probability 1/n. Continuous uniform gives each point probability 0 and each interval probability length/(b − a). Do not mix them.

quiz.a: f(x) = 1/(b − a) for a ≤ x ≤ b; f(x) = 0 outside [a,b].

quiz.q: What is P(X = c) for a continuous uniform X?
quiz.a: 0. A point has zero width, so zero area.

quiz.q: Why is the height of the uniform density equal to 1/(b − a)?
quiz.a: Total area must be 1. Height × width = h(b − a). So h = 1/(b − a).

quiz.q: X ~ U(0,20). Find P(5 < X < 15), E(X), and Var(X).
A bus comes every 12 minutes. Your wait W is uniform on (0,12). Find P(W > 9) and the 90th percentile of W.
Compare U(0,10) and U(5,15) for P(6 < X < 8) and variance.
quiz.a: Both intervals have length 10, so both densities are 0.1. P(6 < X < 8) = 2/10 = 0.2 for both. Variance is 100/12 ≈ 8.33 for both; only the mean shifts, from 5 to 10. Uniform shape depends on length, not location.

quiz.q: For X ~ U(0,b), P(X ≤ 4) = 0.5. Find b.
quiz.a: F(4) = 4/b = 0.5, so b = 8. The midpoint is 4.

beyond: Not for the exam. Random number generators produce U(0,1) values. Inverse transform sampling turns such a value U into a draw from another distribution by solving F(x) = U. Monte Carlo integration uses many uniform draws to estimate areas and averages. Search for inverse transform sampling, pseudo-random number generator, and Monte Carlo integration.
